title: Kirchhoff's Laws, Wheatstone Bridge and Potentiometer
subcategory: Current Electricity — Kirchhoff's Laws, Wheatstone Bridge, Meter Bridge, Potentiometer

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Current Electricity

summary: Kirchhoff's two laws (charge and energy conservation applied to circuits) let complex networks that plain series/parallel rules can't handle be solved systematically; the Wheatstone bridge and potentiometer are classic balanced-condition applications for measuring unknown resistance and emf.
explanation: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL/junction rule) states the algebraic sum of currents meeting at a junction is zero — a direct statement of conservation of charge (charge can't accumulate at a junction in steady state). Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL/loop rule) states the algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero — a statement of conservation of energy (a charge returning to its starting point has the same potential energy). These two laws are needed (instead of simple series/parallel reduction) whenever a circuit has multiple EMF sources or a network that can't be reduced by inspection, such as a Wheatstone bridge. A Wheatstone bridge has four resistances arranged in a diamond, with a galvanometer connecting the midpoints of two arms; it is 'balanced' (galvanometer shows zero deflection) when P/Q = R/S — at balance, the bridge is completely insensitive to the EMF of the source, only the RATIO of resistances matters, which is what makes it extremely precise for finding an unknown resistance. The meter bridge is a practical, simplified Wheatstone bridge using a uniform 1 m resistance wire, where the balance point (found by sliding a jockey) directly gives the unknown resistance via the wire's length ratio. A potentiometer measures potential difference or emf by comparing it against a known potential gradient along a uniform wire carrying a steady current, WITHOUT drawing any current from the source being measured at balance — this makes it, in principle, more accurate than a voltmeter (which always draws some current, however small, and hence disturbs the very quantity it measures).
commonMisconceptions: Trying to reduce a Wheatstone bridge circuit using plain series-parallel resistor combination rules — the bridge (in its general, unbalanced state) genuinely requires Kirchhoff's laws; only AT balance does the galvanometer branch effectively carry no current and permit simplification.

Assuming a voltmeter can measure emf exactly like a potentiometer — a voltmeter always draws a small current (finite resistance), causing a small unavoidable error, whereas a potentiometer at balance draws zero current from the source under test.
Forgetting sign conventions (direction of current assumed vs. direction of traversal) when applying KVL — a very common source of numerical errors in loop equations.
examples: A metre bridge experiment finds an unknown resistance by locating the null point on the bridge wire and using the known resistance in the other gap.
A potentiometer is used to compare the EMFs of two cells precisely, because it draws no current from either cell at the balance point.
genZNote: Wheatstone bridge at balance: zero current through the galvanometer, maximum precision unlocked.
